title: Ensemble Modeling for Time Series Forecasting: an Adaptive Robust Optimization Approach
claim: Forecasts from individual models drift over time, so we adapt ensemble weights from recent errors and gain consistent error reductions over the best single model.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: problem plot, method equations, result bars
description: A three-panel horizontal figure. Panel (a), "Forecasts drift over time", is a line plot of a bold black target series against an orange Model 1 and five thinner multicolored lines for Models 2 to 6. Model 1 drifts above the target in the second half. A blue shaded band marks the past τ errors, and a dashed vertical line marks time t. Panel (b), "Adaptive Ridge", stacks a red-blue heatmap labeled Z_t (m models × last τ errors). Arrows lead down to a shaded box with β_t = β_0 + V_0 Z_t, then to ŷ_t = X_t^T β_t, with a small caption on how β_0 and V_0 are fitted. Panel (c), "Error reduction vs. best model", is a set of paired horizontal bars in dark and light blue. They show RMSE and CVaR 15% reductions for four case studies, from 14% to 28%.
caption: Overview. (a) Six models forecast one target (data from the wind-speed case study, Section 3.2); Model 1 drifts in the second half. (b) Adaptive Ridge sets the weights βt as an affine function of the models’ last τ errors, with β0 and V0 fitted once by adaptive robust optimization. (c) Reduction in RMSE and CVaR 15% relative to the best single model in each case study.
abstract: Accurate time-series forecasting is critical for many problems involving temporal data. Ensemble modeling is a well-established technique that leverages multiple predictive models to improve accuracy and robustness, since a single predictor's performance can vary widely due to shifts in the underlying data distribution. This paper proposes a new methodology for building robust ensembles of time series forecasting models. Our approach uses Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to construct a linear regression ensemble whose model weights adapt over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through synthetic experiments covering eight disturbance scenarios, from no drift to abrupt regime shifts, and real-world applications, including air pollution management, energy consumption forecasting, and tropical cyclone intensity forecasting. In the real-world applications, our adaptive ensembles outperform the best ensemble member in hindsight by 16-26% in root mean square error (RMSE) and 14-28% in conditional value at risk at the 15% level and improve over the other ensemble methods we compare on most metrics. In the synthetic experiments, they have lower mean RMSE than a rolling-ridge comparator in seven of the eight scenarios, significantly in four, while an abrupt regime shift that first appears after model selection remains a limitation.
